output.title: Designing against positioning drift: pick one workflow to test
output.body:
If you want to design against positioning drift, treat it as one bounded workflow decision: what is the one customer problem or outcome your business says it consistently solves? That is the positioning anchor. Everything else gets checked against it.

For a small business, the question is not whether you can write better copy. It is whether your current workflow keeps sending mixed signals. Start with one repeatable place where drift shows up: how you triage customer inquiries, how you answer sales questions, or how you negotiate project scope. Pick the one that causes confusion most often.

Write the anchor in plain English, then use it as a manual check in that workflow for a short period. If the same questions keep coming up, or scope keeps expanding in ways that pull you off-message, you have found a useful control point. If the workflow stays consistent, the anchor is probably doing its job.

AI can help later by enforcing that wording inside documents, email, CRM, or back-office workflows, but only after the owner has confirmed the anchor is clear and aligned. Bareni’s own knowledge assistant is only a self-built local demo on synthetic data, with the public route locked, so this is still a human decision first. Automation is for consistency, not authority. Useful, if not glamorous.

Which workflow in your business surfaces positioning ambiguity most often? Start there first.
